messages.content: I want to generate synchronized audio from silent video, but I also want to distinguish sound events determined by what is visible from sounds that remain acoustically ambiguous.

That distinction is central to the goal. The video can constrain when a visible event occurs without necessarily determining exactly what it sounds like. The generated audio should stay synchronized with visible events while allowing for sound alternatives where the visual evidence does not settle the acoustic details.
What does synchronization mean in this goal?

The stated timing requirement concerns visible-event audio onset error: the audio associated with a visible event should begin closer to that event’s visual timing. The target is to reduce that onset error by 20% compared with an equally sized deterministic video-to-audio baseline.
So the comparison is against a deterministic baseline of the same size?

Yes. Both qualifications matter: the comparator is a deterministic video-to-audio baseline, and it is equally sized. The 20% target is a reduction in visible-event audio onset error relative to that baseline, not an absolute timing value such as 20 milliseconds.
Does the goal say what the current onset error is?
No. It specifies a relative improvement target, but gives no current error value or measurement unit. Nor does it state that the improvement has already been achieved.
How does the ambiguity part fit with a timing target? Could an event be clear visually but unclear acoustically?

Yes. A visible event may provide a clear cue about when associated audio should start while leaving more than one sound plausible. The goal calls for keeping that timing relationship precise without treating every acoustic detail as uniquely determined by the silent video.
I also want to cover the alternatives, not just acknowledge that they exist.

The stated coverage target is 90% of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples. That confines the target to alternatives supported by the references; it is not a demand to include every sound one could imagine.
Does covering alternatives mean putting every possible sound into one generated track?

Not necessarily. The requirement describes coverage of reference-supported alternatives across samples. It does not specify that all alternatives must play simultaneously in a single output, or prescribe a particular way of representing them.
And the alternatives still have to respect what the video rules out?

Yes. The separate constraint is to keep visually contradicted events below 5%. Accommodating acoustic ambiguity should not become a reason to introduce sound events that conflict with the visible evidence.
Is a sound visually contradicted whenever the video fails to show its source clearly?

Those are different ideas. An unclear or unseen source can leave a sound ambiguous; that alone does not establish visual contradiction. The constraint concerns events that conflict with what is visible, while the coverage target concerns alternatives supported by the references.
So neither visual uncertainty nor reference support can be ignored.

Right. The aim is to distinguish what the video fixes from what it leaves open, while retaining the stated boundaries: 90% coverage of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples and visually contradicted events below 5%.
Would it be accurate to describe the 90% as a per-video requirement?
No. The wording says “across samples.” It does not impose a separate 90% target on each individual video.
What about the below-5% limit—is that the same thing as allowing 5% unsupported alternatives?
No. The stated limit is specifically for visually contradicted events, and it is below 5%, not equal to 5%. The node does not define it as a general allowance for unsupported alternatives.
Can you put the two numerical requirements side by side without merging them?

For timing, reduce visible-event audio onset error by 20% versus an equally sized deterministic video-to-audio baseline. For alternatives, cover 90% of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples, while keeping visually contradicted events below 5%. They address related but distinct aspects of the goal.
Would meeting the onset target alone be enough to describe the full goal as met?

No. Better onset alignment addresses synchronization, but the stated goal also requires distinguishing visually determined sound events from acoustically ambiguous alternatives. The alternative-coverage and visual-contradiction thresholds remain separate requirements.
And covering many alternatives alone would not establish that the audio is synchronized?

Correct. Broad coverage does not, by itself, establish a 20% reduction in visible-event audio onset error relative to the equally sized deterministic baseline. The goal calls for both timing improvement and appropriate treatment of acoustic ambiguity.
How should I phrase the overall aim without implying that any of these targets have already been reached?

You could say: “The goal is to generate synchronized audio from silent video, distinguishing visually determined sound events from acoustically ambiguous alternatives. It targets a 20% reduction in visible-event audio onset error relative to an equally sized deterministic video-to-audio baseline, 90% coverage of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples, and visually contradicted events below 5%.”
How would you approach the distinction between visually determined sounds and acoustically ambiguous alternatives?

The proposal separates their roles. It anchors visually determined audio onsets to tracked motion and contact peaks, while using diffusion to sample acoustically ambiguous alternatives with visual-consistency filtering. That keeps the timing cues supplied by the video distinct from acoustic details the video leaves open.
What exactly is being anchored?

The audio onsets for visually determined events—the points where their associated sounds begin. Tracked motion and contact peaks provide visual timing cues for those onsets. The proposal does not say that every aspect of a generated sound is fixed by those cues.
Why mention both tracked motion and contact peaks?

They describe the visual evidence to which the proposal would relate onset timing: motion as it is tracked over time, and peaks associated with contact. The proposal names both, but does not prescribe a rule for weighing them or require that every onset have both kinds of cue.
Does a contact peak tell us the exact sound to generate?

Not by itself. In this proposal, contact peaks help anchor visually determined onset timing. The acoustic character of a sound can still be ambiguous even when the video offers a useful cue about when it should begin.
So the diffusion part handles that ambiguity?

Yes. Diffusion is proposed for sampling alternatives where the acoustic outcome is ambiguous. Visual-consistency filtering then constrains those alternatives so that accommodating uncertainty does not mean accepting events that conflict with the video.
Are those sampled alternatives meant to change the visually determined onset?

The proposal does not frame them that way. It gives visually determined audio onsets their own anchor in tracked motion and contact peaks, and uses diffusion for ambiguous alternatives. It does not specify how all timing and acoustic choices are combined in a final output.
What does visual-consistency filtering check here?

At the level stated, it checks sampled alternatives against what is visible and filters for visual consistency. The proposal does not define a particular test, threshold, or implementation for that filtering.
Is visual consistency the same as saying there is only one possible sound?
No. More than one acoustic alternative may remain consistent with the same silent video. Filtering is meant to rule out visual conflicts, not erase ambiguity that the visual evidence cannot resolve.
Could you explain the contrast without assuming any particular scene?

A visible motion or contact may provide a cue for an associated audio onset. Even with that onset anchored, the video may not settle all the sound’s acoustic details. The proposal uses the visual cue for the determined timing and samples alternatives for what remains acoustically ambiguous, subject to visual-consistency filtering.
Does the proposal say how to decide whether an event is visually determined in the first place?
No. It states what to do with visually determined onsets and acoustically ambiguous alternatives, but does not specify a classification procedure for separating them.
Does it specify a tracking method or a particular diffusion model?

No. It calls for tracked motion and contact peaks as onset anchors, and diffusion with visual-consistency filtering for sampling alternatives. It leaves the tracking method, diffusion configuration, and filtering implementation unspecified.
Would you call this a measured improvement in synchronization?

No. It is a proposal for addressing synchronization and ambiguity, not a reported experiment or measured result. Anchoring onsets to visual cues describes the intended approach; it does not establish that any timing target has been achieved.
And sampling alternatives does not itself prove the desired coverage?

Correct. Sampling gives a proposed way to represent acoustic ambiguity. The proposal supplies no results showing how many reference-supported alternatives it covers or how often visually contradicted events occur.
I want to make sure the filtering does not get described as replacing the onset anchors.

They serve different purposes in the proposal. Tracked motion and contact peaks anchor visually determined audio onsets; visual-consistency filtering constrains the alternatives sampled with diffusion. Neither is stated as a substitute for the other.
Is it fair to say the video has a stronger role for onset timing than for ambiguous acoustic detail?

That captures the proposal’s distinction, with one qualification: it applies to the visually determined onsets and acoustically ambiguous alternatives named here, not as a claim about every possible video or sound. The proposal anchors the former to tracked motion and contact peaks while allowing the latter to be sampled within visual constraints.
Then give me a concise formulation of the proposed approach.

Anchor visually determined audio onsets to tracked motion and contact peaks; use diffusion to sample acoustically ambiguous sound alternatives, with visual-consistency filtering to constrain those alternatives.
What contact-confidence threshold anchors visible onsets without suppressing reference-supported sound alternatives?

That remains an open question. No numerical contact-confidence threshold is specified. The intended balance is to use sufficiently credible contact cues to anchor visible-event audio onsets without treating a less certain contact cue as a reason to discard sound alternatives supported by the references.
What is the threshold deciding in that formulation?

It would decide when confidence in a visible contact is sufficient to use that contact as an onset anchor. The question also asks whether that choice leaves room for reference-supported sound alternatives. It does not define the confidence measure or specify a threshold value.
Would a higher threshold always be safer?

Not necessarily. A higher threshold demands stronger contact evidence before anchoring an onset, but could leave some visible onsets without a contact-based anchor. Whether it also suppresses alternatives depends on how that threshold is used. The question asks for a balance rather than declaring that the highest possible threshold is best.
Then would a low threshold be better for onset coverage?

A lower threshold could admit more candidate contact cues, but admitting a cue is not the same as showing that it is a reliable onset anchor. The question does not provide evidence that a lower value improves timing or preserves the reference-supported alternatives.
I am trying to separate two possible effects: missing an anchor and suppressing an alternative. Are they the same?

No. Missing an anchor concerns whether a visible onset gets tied to a contact cue. Suppressing an alternative concerns whether a reference-supported sound possibility remains available. The question connects these concerns, but it does not say that one automatically causes the other.
So the threshold might be useful for timing without deciding the sound’s exact acoustic identity?

Yes, that is the distinction to preserve. Confidence in a visible contact could bear on where to anchor an onset without proving that only one acoustic realization is possible. An onset anchor need not eliminate reference-supported alternatives whose acoustic details remain ambiguous.
Could we simply set a confidence percentage now?

The supplied question gives no basis for selecting one. A percentage would be a new numerical choice, not an answer established by the current information. The contact-confidence scale itself is also unspecified, so a bare number would be especially hard to interpret.
Is the contact-confidence threshold the same as the below-5% limit on visually contradicted events?

No. Contact confidence concerns when to anchor a visible onset to a contact cue. The below-5% limit concerns visually contradicted events. They address different things, and nothing here equates their numerical values.
Does the 90% coverage target supply the missing threshold?

No. The 90% target concerns coverage of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples. It helps express what the threshold must not undermine, but it does not specify a contact-confidence cutoff.
And the 20% onset-error reduction target does not tell us the cutoff either?

Correct. That target describes the desired reduction in visible-event audio onset error relative to an equally sized deterministic video-to-audio baseline. It is not a contact-confidence value. The open question is which threshold, if any, supports onset anchoring without suppressing reference-supported alternatives.
What would count as answering the question, as opposed to just restating it?

An answer would identify a contact-confidence threshold on a defined confidence scale and establish that using it anchors visible onsets while preserving reference-supported sound alternatives. The present information does neither, so the threshold should remain unspecified rather than be guessed.
Could the threshold be interpreted as a blanket rule that anything below it must be silent?

That would go beyond the question. Failing to qualify a contact cue as an onset anchor does not, by itself, establish that no reference-supported sound alternative is possible. Treating the threshold as a silence rule could conflate uncertainty about visible contact with the absence of sound.
What if the contact cue is confident but the sound is still ambiguous?

Those can coexist. A confident visible contact could provide an onset anchor while multiple acoustic alternatives remain reference-supported. The threshold question is precisely about anchoring visible onsets without allowing the anchoring rule to suppress those alternatives.
So for now, what is the most accurate short statement?

The appropriate contact-confidence threshold is undetermined: it must anchor visible audio onsets without suppressing reference-supported sound alternatives, but no threshold value or confidence scale has been specified.
Suppose we use a 0.8 contact-confidence gate. Could that answer the threshold question?

It gives a candidate answer, but only as a hypothesis: a 0.8 contact-confidence gate will cut visible-event audio onset error by 20% while preserving 90% coverage of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples and keeping visually contradicted events under 5%. Those outcomes have not been established.
What does the 0.8 govern?

It is the proposed contact-confidence threshold for deciding when a visible contact cue qualifies as an onset anchor. The hypothesis does not define the confidence scale or specify how confidence is calculated.
Does 0.8 mean that 80% of visible contacts would qualify?

No. A threshold value is not a statement about the proportion of contacts that pass it. The hypothesis gives no distribution of contact-confidence values, so it does not tell us how many cues would qualify.
Could I describe the 0.8 as an 80% probability that contact occurred?

Not on the information given. The value is called a contact-confidence gate, but the hypothesis does not say that the confidence score is a calibrated probability. It is safer to retain the term “0.8 contact-confidence gate” without assigning it that interpretation.
How is the gate supposed to help synchronization?

The hypothesis is that using the gate to select contact cues for anchoring visible audio onsets will cut onset error by 20%. It proposes that relationship; it does not report a measured reduction or explain the precise mechanism by which that value would produce it.
For that 20%, should I read it as an absolute amount of time?

No. It is a proposed percentage reduction in onset error. In the stated goal, the timing comparison is against an equally sized deterministic video-to-audio baseline. Neither an absolute error nor a time unit is supplied here.
What does “preserving 90% alternative coverage” add to the hypothesis?

It says the proposed onset-anchoring threshold should not come at the expense of the goal’s coverage of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples. The hypothesis predicts that 90% coverage can be retained alongside the 20% onset-error reduction.
Does that imply 90% coverage for every individual sample?
No. The coverage requirement is across samples. The hypothesis does not specify a per-sample coverage rate or say that every sample must contain the same number of alternatives.
And alternatives means any sound that might conceivably fit?
No. The stated coverage concerns reference-supported sound alternatives. The hypothesis does not extend the target to every imaginable sound.
I’m concerned that a contact-confidence gate could be taken to reject all sounds when confidence is below 0.8.

That would add a rule the hypothesis does not state. The 0.8 gate is proposed for contact-based onset anchoring; it is not described as a blanket test for whether any sound may exist. In particular, failing to qualify as a contact anchor does not by itself rule out a reference-supported sound alternative.
So a qualified contact anchor and multiple sound alternatives can coexist?
Yes. The hypothesis combines contact-based onset anchoring with preservation of alternative coverage. It does not require a qualified contact cue to determine one unique acoustic realization.
Where does the under-5% condition fit?

It is the hypothesis’s visual-consistency constraint: visually contradicted events are predicted to remain under 5%. That is distinct from the 90% coverage figure. The proposal aims to retain supported alternatives without admitting too many events that conflict with the video.
Is “under 5%” interchangeable with “5% or less”?
No. “Under 5%” means strictly below 5%. Saying “5% or less” would also allow exactly 5%, which is not what this hypothesis states.
Does the hypothesis specify how visual contradictions are identified?

No. It predicts an under-5% rate of visually contradicted events, but does not define a detection procedure or a measurement denominator. Those details should not be inferred from the percentage alone.
Can we say that diffusion and visual-consistency filtering guarantee those numbers?

No. The proposed approach uses diffusion to sample ambiguous alternatives with visual-consistency filtering, but this hypothesis does not establish a guarantee from those components. The 20%, 90%, and under-5% figures are predicted outcomes for the 0.8 gate, not demonstrated consequences.
Does the hypothesis actually resolve the earlier question about which threshold works?
It nominates 0.8 as a threshold that is hypothesized to work. It does not establish that 0.8 achieves the stated balance, nor does it compare that threshold with other values.
Would calling 0.8 the optimal threshold go too far?
Yes. The hypothesis neither tests other thresholds nor claims optimality. It proposes that a 0.8 contact-confidence gate will meet the stated timing, coverage, and visual-contradiction conditions.
If the timing prediction held but alternative coverage did not, would that still match this hypothesis in full?

No. This is a combined hypothesis: a 20% onset-error reduction, preservation of 90% reference-supported alternative coverage across samples, and visually contradicted events under 5%. A timing outcome alone would not establish the entire claim.
Likewise, coverage without the onset-error reduction would be incomplete?

Correct. Preserving alternatives is only one part of the predicted outcome. The hypothesis also includes the 20% reduction in visible-event audio onset error and the under-5% visual-contradiction condition.
Give me wording that keeps the threshold and every numerical prediction explicit without presenting them as results.

The hypothesis is that a 0.8 contact-confidence gate will reduce visible-event audio onset error by 20% relative to the equally sized deterministic video-to-audio baseline, preserve 90% coverage of reference-supported sound alternatives across samples, and keep visually contradicted events under 5%. These are predictions, not reported results.
How can we investigate which contact-confidence threshold anchors visible onsets without suppressing reference-supported sound alternatives?

The plan is to sweep contact-confidence gates from 0.6 to 0.9 on MultiSound-AV, measuring onset MAE, alternative coverage, and visual contradictions. That would let the timing and alternative-related measurements be considered together across the gates evaluated.
What does it mean to sweep the gates?

It means evaluating multiple contact-confidence gate settings within the stated 0.6-to-0.9 range rather than relying on a single setting. The plan does not specify the increments, the number of settings, or an exact list of values to evaluate.
So should I list 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, and 0.9 as the planned settings?
Not as a definite list. Those are possible values within the range, but the plan states only a sweep from 0.6 to 0.9. It does not prescribe steps of 0.1.
And 0.8 is within the range, but is it definitely one of the evaluated gates?

It is within the stated range. Whether it is an evaluated setting depends on the sweep’s unspecified choice of values, so the plan alone does not guarantee that 0.8 is included as a discrete test point.
What role does MultiSound-AV play here?
MultiSound-AV is the named dataset on which the gate sweep is planned. Nothing in this plan specifies its size, contents, splits, or how its references are organized.
What exactly are the three measurements?

They are onset MAE, alternative coverage, and visual contradictions. Together, they address onset timing, retention of sound alternatives, and conflict with the video. The plan names these measurements without specifying their full calculation procedures.
Can you unpack onset MAE without assuming a result?

MAE stands for mean absolute error. Here it refers to error in audio onset timing. The plan is to measure it for the gate settings, but it gives no measured MAE values, timing units, or details about how onsets are matched for calculation.
Does a smaller onset MAE generally mean better timing alignment?

Yes: for a given onset-error measurement, a smaller mean absolute error indicates smaller average absolute timing deviations. That explains how to read the metric; it does not predict what the MultiSound-AV sweep will show.
How should I read alternative coverage in this plan?

It is the measurement relevant to retaining reference-supported sound alternatives while varying the contact-confidence gate. The plan does not specify its counting procedure or give a coverage value for any gate.
And visual contradictions?

That measurement concerns generated sound events that conflict with what is visible. The plan says to measure visual contradictions alongside onset MAE and alternative coverage, but does not specify a counting rule or report a value.
Why measure all three instead of just finding the gate with the lowest onset MAE?

The threshold question has more than a timing component: it asks for an onset anchor that does not suppress reference-supported sound alternatives. Measuring alternative coverage alongside onset MAE keeps that concern visible, while measuring visual contradictions keeps track of whether the sound events conflict with the video. The plan does not say that the lowest-MAE gate should automatically be selected.
Does the sweep itself decide which threshold is best?
No selection rule is specified. The plan calls for measurements across a range of gates; it does not define how to rank competing outcomes or commit to a final threshold.
Can I already say that increasing the gate improves visual consistency?
No. The plan provides no results or predicted trend across the 0.6-to-0.9 range. Visual contradictions are something to measure, not an outcome the sweep has already established.
Likewise, it does not say whether alternative coverage rises or falls across that range?
Correct. Coverage is an observation the plan calls for at the evaluated gate settings. No direction or magnitude of change is stated.
Does this plan specify whether the contact-confidence score is a calibrated probability?
No. It names contact-confidence gates and their range, but does not define the underlying score or say that a value such as 0.6 represents a 60% probability.
Does it specify a particular motion tracker, diffusion configuration, or visual-consistency filter for the sweep?
No. The stated plan is limited to sweeping contact-confidence gates on MultiSound-AV and measuring the three named outcomes. It does not provide those implementation details.
Could I say the sweep has already established whether the timing and coverage goals can coexist?

No. This is a plan, not a completed experiment. It identifies measurements that bear on timing, alternatives, and visual contradictions, but reports no findings about whether any gate achieves the desired combination.
What is the most precise one-sentence description of the plan?
Sweep contact-confidence gates from 0.6 to 0.9 on MultiSound-AV, measuring onset MAE, alternative coverage, and visual contradictions, without presuming which gate the measurements will favor.
What activity would evaluate the contact-confidence gate on MultiSound-AV?

Run contact-gate sweeps from 0.6 to 0.9 on MultiSound-AV against a size-matched deterministic baseline, measuring onset MAE, alternative recall, and contradiction rate. That is the activity to carry out; no sweep results are stated.
What does “against a size-matched deterministic baseline” add?

It identifies the comparator for the sweep: a deterministic baseline matched in size. The comparison should not be described as one against an arbitrary baseline. The activity does not specify how size is measured or give any baseline scores.
Are we running just the two endpoints, 0.6 and 0.9?
Not necessarily. A sweep means considering gate settings across the 0.6–0.9 range, but the activity does not list the settings, their spacing, or how many runs there will be.
Would it be safe to say the sweep definitely includes 0.8?

The range includes 0.8, but the activity does not give a discrete list of evaluated settings. It would be more precise to say the sweep spans 0.6–0.9 than to assert that any particular intermediate value is included.
How is this activity connected to the proposed 0.8 gate?

The sweep is intended to evaluate that gate hypothesis by measuring timing, recovery of sound alternatives, and visual contradictions across contact-gate settings. It does not, on its own, confirm the hypothesis or report what happens at 0.8.
Can you distinguish the three measurements without giving them results?

Onset MAE concerns the magnitude of onset-timing errors. Alternative recall concerns how many reference-supported sound alternatives are recovered. Contradiction rate concerns how often sound events contradict the visible evidence. The activity calls for measuring all three; it reports no values for any of them.
What does MAE stand for here?
Mean absolute error. In this activity it applies to audio onset timing. The stated activity does not specify a timing unit, a matching procedure for onsets, or an observed MAE.
Why not measure onset MAE alone?

Onset MAE addresses synchronization, but not whether sound alternatives are retained or whether events conflict with the video. Measuring alternative recall and contradiction rate alongside it keeps those distinct aspects in view during the contact-gate sweep.
Is alternative recall simply a count of how many different sounds get generated?

No. “Recall” relates the recovered alternatives to reference-supported alternatives, rather than rewarding variety for its own sake. The activity does not provide the precise counting or matching rule, so it would be premature to turn that description into a specific formula.
And is contradiction rate the percentage of outputs that sound unusual?

No. The relevant issue is contradiction with what is visible, not whether an output sounds unusual. Although the activity calls the measurement a rate, it does not define its denominator or give a measured percentage.
Could a gate have good onset MAE and still need scrutiny on the other two measures?

Yes. The measurements capture different properties. A timing measurement alone would not tell us its alternative recall or contradiction rate. That is why the activity includes all three rather than treating onset MAE as a complete evaluation.
Does the baseline have to be deterministic, or is size matching the only condition?
Both are stated conditions: the baseline is deterministic and size-matched. Neither qualification should be dropped when describing the comparison.
Do we know the baseline’s architecture, size, or performance?
No. The activity specifies a size-matched deterministic baseline but provides no architecture, size value, or performance measurements.
Does “run” mean the sweeps have already been completed?
No. It states the activity to perform. There are no reported MultiSound-AV measurements or conclusions in this node.
Can we already say which contact-gate setting minimizes onset MAE?
No. That would require results from the sweep. The 0.6–0.9 range and the choice of metrics do not establish how onset MAE varies across gate settings.
Nor can we say which setting gives the highest alternative recall?
Correct. Alternative recall is to be measured, not inferred from the gate values alone. The activity states no trend or winning setting.
What about the contradiction rate—should we expect it to fall as the gate rises?
The activity does not state a direction of change. Contradiction rate is one of the observations to collect across the sweep, so a claimed trend would go beyond what is supplied.
Does the activity prescribe how to identify contact peaks or calculate contact confidence?

No. It specifies the contact-gate range, MultiSound-AV, the size-matched deterministic comparator, and the three measurements. It does not specify how contact confidence is produced or how contact peaks are identified.
If I describe this in one sentence, which details must remain explicit?

Say that the activity is to run 0.6–0.9 contact-gate sweeps on MultiSound-AV against a size-matched deterministic baseline, measuring onset MAE, alternative recall, and contradiction rate. That keeps the range, dataset, comparator, and all three measurements explicit without implying that results are available.
What did the 0.8 contact-confidence gate measure on MultiSound-AV?

On MultiSound-AV, the 0.8 gate achieved 78-ms onset MAE, compared with 100-ms onset MAE for the size-matched deterministic baseline. It also recorded 92% alternative recall and 3.8% visual contradictions.
Can you separate the timing comparison from the other two figures?

The timing comparison is 78 ms of onset mean absolute error for the 0.8 gate versus 100 ms for the baseline. The other figures describe the 0.8 gate: 92% alternative recall and 3.8% visual contradictions. No baseline figures for those two measures are stated.
What is the difference between the two onset MAE values?
The difference is 22 ms: 100 ms minus 78 ms. Relative to the baseline’s 100-ms onset MAE, that is a 22% reduction in the reported onset MAE.
Does the 78 ms mean every generated onset was 78 ms away from its visual event?

No. MAE is a mean absolute error, so 78 ms is an aggregate onset-error measure, not a claim that every individual onset had the same error. The evidence does not give the distribution of individual errors.
Is that 78-ms figure the sound’s duration?
No. It measures error in onset timing, not sound duration. The corresponding baseline onset MAE is 100 ms.
What exactly does the 92% tell us?

It is the reported alternative recall for the 0.8 gate on MultiSound-AV. It concerns recovery of sound alternatives, not the timing error or the rate of visual contradictions. The evidence does not give a per-sample breakdown.
Could I call that 92% alternative precision?
No. The reported metric is alternative recall. Precision would be a different measure, and no alternative-precision value is provided.
Does 92% mean each video yielded 92% of its possible sounds?

That does not follow from the reported figure. It is an aggregate alternative-recall result; the evidence does not say what recall was for any individual video or define a set of every conceivable sound.
And how should I state the visual result?
State it as 3.8% visual contradictions for the 0.8 gate on MultiSound-AV. It is a reported contradiction rate, not a timing error or an alternative-recall figure.
Does 3.8% tell us how many contradictory events there were?
Not without the underlying count and denominator. The evidence provides the percentage, but not the number of events or samples used to calculate it.
Can we compare the contradiction rate with the baseline’s?
Not from these figures. The baseline is given a 100-ms onset MAE, but no baseline contradiction rate is stated. The same limitation applies to a baseline alternative-recall comparison.
Do we know how the other gate settings in the sweep performed?

No. This evidence reports outcomes for the 0.8 gate and the baseline timing comparison. It gives no measurements for other contact-gate settings, so it cannot establish which gate performed best across the sweep.
Could the reported onset difference be attributed solely to choosing the 0.8 threshold?
The evidence reports a comparison; it does not isolate the threshold as the sole cause of the difference. It supplies no further analysis of what produced the observed onset MAE values.
Do these figures include uncertainty intervals or variability across samples?

No uncertainty intervals or sample-level variability are stated. The reported figures are 78-ms onset MAE for the 0.8 gate, 100-ms onset MAE for the baseline, 92% alternative recall, and 3.8% visual contradictions.
Please give me a compact results sentence that preserves the dataset, comparator, and all three measurements.
On MultiSound-AV, the 0.8 contact-confidence gate recorded 78-ms onset MAE versus 100 ms for the size-matched deterministic baseline, with 92% alternative recall and 3.8% visual contradictions.
How should we evaluate the 0.8 gate when contact is occluded?

Evaluate the 0.8 contact-confidence gate on held-out MultiSound-AV occlusions against a size-matched baseline, measuring onset MAE, alternative recall, and visual contradictions. This states an evaluation activity, not its outcome.
What does “held-out” tell us here?
It identifies the MultiSound-AV occlusions as held-out material for this evaluation. The activity does not specify how they were held out, how many there are, or what forms the occlusions take.
Is this another sweep over contact-confidence gates?
No sweep is specified here. This activity evaluates the 0.8 gate in particular on held-out MultiSound-AV occlusions.
Why keep the baseline size-matched?

Size matching is an explicit condition of the comparison. It means the evaluation should be described as comparing the 0.8 gate with a size-matched baseline, rather than with an unspecified comparator. The activity does not define the size measure or describe the baseline further.
Should we call that baseline deterministic?
This activity calls it a size-matched baseline. It does not independently specify whether it is deterministic, so I would not add that qualification when stating this evaluation.
What are we checking with onset MAE on these occlusions?

Onset MAE measures average absolute error in onset timing for this evaluation. It is the timing measure to collect for the 0.8 gate and its comparison with the size-matched baseline. No onset MAE value is given for the held-out occlusions.
Would the onset MAE tell us whether every onset is well aligned?
Not by itself. A mean absolute error summarizes timing deviations; it does not give the error for every individual onset. The activity does not call for a per-onset breakdown.
What does alternative recall contribute?

It keeps the evaluation attentive to recovery of reference-supported sound alternatives, not just onset timing. The activity names alternative recall as a measure but provides neither a value nor a detailed calculation rule for the held-out occlusions.
Could a low onset MAE alone answer whether the gate preserves sound alternatives?

No. Onset MAE and alternative recall address different questions. Measuring both makes it possible to examine timing and recovery of alternatives separately, without treating good timing as proof of good recall.
And why record visual contradictions as well?
They address whether sound events conflict with what is visible. Alternative recall alone would not settle that question, so visual contradictions are a separate named measure in the activity.
Does the activity say how a contradiction will be counted?
No. It says to measure visual contradictions, but does not define a counting procedure, denominator, or reported rate for this held-out evaluation.
Can we infer that occlusion will make contact confidence lower?
Not as a reported fact here. The evaluation concerns held-out occlusions, but the activity gives no contact-confidence measurements or trend under those conditions.
Should we expect the 0.8 gate to perform worse there?
The activity does not state an expected direction. Onset MAE, alternative recall, and visual contradictions are to be measured on the held-out occlusions; their values are not supplied.
Does this tell us whether the gate meets its proposed targets on occlusions?
Not yet. It specifies what to evaluate and what to measure, but gives no held-out-occlusion results from which to assess those targets.
Can we carry over measurements from other MultiSound-AV samples as the result for this evaluation?
